# Automatic Summaries with the `apa_descriptives` Function

The first table of most empirical papers describes the sample. `apa_descriptives` makes this table: for each continuous variable, its mean and standard deviation, *M* (*SD*), and for each categorical variable, the number and percentage of respondents at each level, *n* (%). Numeric variables are treated as continuous, and factors, character vectors, and logical vectors as categorical. Each categorical variable has a heading row, with its levels indented below it.

## Data Set Summaries

The `survey` data set in the MASS package [@ripleyMASSSupportFunctions2009] has the answers of 237 statistics students to a short questionnaire. Without groups, there is one column for the whole sample:

```{r}
#| label: survey
d_survey <- MASS::survey |>
  mutate(
    Exer = fct_recode(
      Exer, 
      Frequently = "Freq") |> 
      fct_relevel("Frequently", after = Inf),
    Smoke = fct_recode(
      Smoke, 
      Occasionally = "Occas", 
      Regularly = "Regul") |> 
      fct_relevel("Heavy", after = Inf)
  ) |> 
  select(Age, 
         `Height (cm)` = Height, 
         `Pulse (beats per minute)` = Pulse, 
         Smoking = Smoke, 
         Exercise = Exer,
         Sex)


apa_descriptives(d_survey, format_variable_names = FALSE) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Variables are named by their formatted names unless `labels` gives better ones. Percentages are of the non-missing responses, and the note lists the number of missing values of each variable that has any.

## Groups

With `by`, each group gets a column, with its size in the header, followed by a column for the whole sample (`total = FALSE` leaves it out). Rows whose group is missing are left out, and the note says how many.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-survey-by-sex
#| tbl-cap: "Characteristics of Students by Sex"
apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  format_variable_names = FALSE,
  by = Sex
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Skewed Variables and Group Differences

Age is strongly skewed in this sample (most students are about 20, a few much older), so its median and interquartile range, *Mdn* (*IQR*), describe it better. `continuous` sets the description of particular variables.

With `test = TRUE`, a *p* column tests the group differences: Welch's *t* test (two groups) or Welch's one-way ANOVA (more groups) for variables described by their mean, the Kruskal–Wallis test for variables described by their median, and the chi-square test of independence for categorical variables. When a categorical variable's table has an expected count below 5, where the chi-square approximation is poor, Fisher's exact test is used for that variable instead, and the note names it (`categorical_test = "chisq"` or `"fisher"` uses one test for all categorical variables). Tests are not shown by default, because many journals discourage testing baseline differences in randomized trials, where any difference is due to chance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-survey-tests
#| apa7-width: landscape
#| tbl-cap: "Characteristics of Students by Sex With Tests of Group Differences"
apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  by = Sex,
  continuous = c(Age = "median_iqr"),
  test = TRUE, 
  format_variable_names = FALSE
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Missing Values and Ranges

By default, the note lists the missing values. With `missing = "row"`, each variable with missing values gets a "Missing" row with the number of missing values in each column instead. With `range = TRUE`, each continuous variable gets a "Range" row with its minimum and maximum:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-survey-missing-range
#| tbl-cap: "Characteristics of Students by Sex With Ranges and Missing Values"
apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  by = Sex,
  missing = "row",
  format_variable_names = FALSE
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Options

* `categorical` treats numeric codes (e.g., 1 = yes, 0 = no) as categories.
* `digits` and `percent_digits` set the decimal places of the statistics and the percentages.
* `format_variable_names = FALSE` keeps unlabeled variable names exactly as they are.

For tables with other layouts, see [Building tables by hand](summarize.html), which shows how to make any data frame into an APA-style table.
